paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

This is about the shared bicycle shed behind the west entrance, not the locked storage room downstairs. I help keep the shed usable because I bike to the library most weekdays, but I am not the building manager and I do not assign spaces. The shed has twelve marked floor spaces, two wall hooks for children’s bikes, a pump mounted beside the door, and a narrow aisle that needs to stay clear. There are eight regular adult riders in the building, though the bikes in the shed change from day to day.

On Tuesday morning, I found the aisle partly blocked by a blue cargo bike and a stack of flattened cardboard. Omar Reyes, who lives in 1A, had moved three bicycles away from the leaking corner after rain came under the door. He put them along the back wall so their tires would not sit in the water. He told me, “I was trying to keep the chains dry, not claim another space.” I could see that his move had kept the bikes out of the puddle, but the cargo bike’s handlebar was now sticking into the aisle. I thanked him for moving the bikes, and he said he would come back after work to shift them again.

The cardboard was a separate issue. It had been left beside the recycling bins after a delivery of replacement door hardware, and nobody had written a name on it. I did not know who brought it into the shed or whether it was waiting to be picked up. I moved only the top piece far enough to get my own bicycle through, then put it back where it had been. I did not throw any of it away. The rain had also left a damp strip near the threshold, but there was no standing water by the time I left for work.

That evening I measured the aisle from the painted line to the opposite rack. It is about three feet wide when no handlebars or boxes stick out, and about twenty inches at the narrowest point with the cargo bike in its Tuesday position. The door opens inward, so a bike leaning behind it can keep the door from opening all the way. The shed light works, although it takes several seconds to come on. I took two photos from the doorway and one photo of the wet corner. The photos show the floor and bike positions; they do not show anyone’s face or apartment number.

I sent a message to Elise Chen, the property manager, asking her to arrange removal of the cardboard and to have maintenance check the door seal at the west entrance. I asked Elise, not Omar, because she handles building repairs and shared-area pickup. I also asked her to confirm whether the back wall is meant to be temporary overflow space or whether residents should keep that area empty. I did not ask her to assign a particular space to me. Elise replied, “I can ask maintenance to inspect the seal on Friday, and I’ll check the pickup schedule.” She did not say when the cardboard would be collected, and I have not treated that as confirmed.

For the next few days, I left the bikes where Omar had placed them, except for moving my own bike in and out without blocking the doorway. On Wednesday, Omar came back as he said he would and turned the cargo bike so its handlebar faced the wall. That opened most of the aisle, but the bike still sat partly across a painted floor mark. He explained that the rear wheel was close to the wet corner and he did not want to rest it against the wall. I did not move his bike or tell him which space to use. I took a fresh photo after he finished, so Elise could see the change from Tuesday.

I checked the shed again on Friday morning before leaving for work. The flattened cardboard was still there, now stacked neatly against the recycling bins, and there was no new leak. The metal strip at the bottom of the door looked damp, but I could not tell whether that was old moisture or water from overnight. Maintenance had not visited by that time. I sent Elise the updated photo and wrote that the aisle was passable but still narrower than the painted line suggested. I asked her to let me know if maintenance found a reason the seal could not be repaired promptly. I did not receive another reply that day.

To make my notes easier to follow, I wrote down the practical points that seem relevant:

1. The three bikes were moved by Omar on Tuesday because water had reached the corner. He moved them along the back wall, and on Wednesday he turned the cargo bike so its handlebar faced the wall. I did not move or claim any of his bikes.
2. The cardboard came from a delivery of door hardware, but I do not know who left it in the shed or whether it is awaiting pickup. I only moved one piece briefly to pass through, and I did not discard any cardboard. It was stacked beside the recycling bins when I checked on Friday.
3. I asked Elise Chen to arrange pickup and a maintenance check, and to clarify the use of the back wall. She said she would check the pickup schedule and that maintenance could inspect the seal on Friday. The inspection was not confirmed as completed when I last checked.

If maintenance does come to inspect the west entrance, the wet corner and the inward-opening door are the two details I hope they look at together. If the seal is repaired, the bikes may be able to return to their usual marked spaces without being kept along the back wall; if it is not repaired, the water could reach that corner again after rain.
